abstract: This review synthesizes three decades of research on whether bilingualism confers an advantage in executive function. Early studies reported a consistent advantage on inhibition tasks, but more recent pre-registered replications find effects that are smaller, depend on context, and are often absent in adults. The current synthesis holds that bilingualism shapes attention selectively, with the clearest effects appearing in switching tasks and in children and older adults. The review closes by proposing a unified model and identifying three open questions for future work.
headline: Review of 30 years of research finding the bilingual executive function advantage is smaller, context-dependent, and often null in adults…
key_points: Early studies consistently reported a bilingual advantage on inhibition tasks.
Recent pre-registered replications find the effects to be smaller, context-dependent, and often null in adults.
The current synthesis holds that bilingualism shapes attention selectively, most clearly on switching tasks.
The strongest effects appear primarily in children and older adults.
The review proposes a unified model to account for these mixed findings.
The review names three open questions to guide future research.
